content_html_sanitized:
Posted May 2, 2001
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Until recently, most Americans have paid little attention to the global context for marijuana prohibition and the broader Drug War. After all, it is a domestic policy and DEAland is The Super Power.

The only foreign interest was in punishing the supply countries who forced their wicked drugs on innocent Americans, who otherwise would have confined themselves to our own wholesome products, Bourbon and tobacco, which we graciously share with the rest of the world.

However, the DEAland government pays a great deal of attention to the drugs policies of other countries, even those as distant and isolated as Australia.
See
Why the US won't let Australia reform its drug laws. The real drug war.

There are two reasons for this interest.

First, prohibitionism is a global ideology, like Communism, and deviation from the party line is a moral threat.

Second, if another country develops successful drugs policies that deviate from prohibitionism the prohibitionist paradigm could be shattered. After all, pragmatism is an American philosophy. Prohibitionism is not just morally superior; it is the only possible policy. Anything else would have to be a disaster. This is why the DEAland Drug Czar had to lie about the success of Dutch cannabis policies.
See
 " The failure of Dutch drug policy " An Examination of Prohibitionist Propaganda and the Official Dutch Government Response -- Special To MarijuanaNews
and links

The fact is that several European countries have been quietly moving away from rigid prohibitionism for several years. However, that is not the same as actively opposing DEAland’s policies. Most European countries have placed great value on cooperation with DEAland on most issues. Many European governments disliked the Vietnam war, but were too dependent on NATO to object too much.

The collapse of the Soviet Union greatly increased the military independence of Europe just as the European Union was emerging as a great economic power. The significance of these developments was muted by the fact that the Europeans were fairly comfortable with most of the policies of the Clinton Administration. However, there is one relevant, recent, exception… the Plan Colombia.

Now, enter Bush.

Although his father was respected by the European leaders, the son looked even more unseasoned to them than to us.

Two recent moves by Bush have confirmed their worst fears. First, he repudiated the Kyoto climate treaty, which was never formally ratified by the Senate. Then he announced that the US would develop a missile defense system -- and unilaterally repudiate the 1972 ABM treaty, although that has not been quite explicitly stated.

Let me emphasize that it does not matter whether these are good or bad decisions. The point is simply that – rightly or wrongly -- the Europeans and others are appalled by these moves. And note, both actions involve unilateral rejections of treaties.

When the 1961 Single Convention was ratified, Harry Anslinger crowed that it meant that marijuana could never be legalized. This and other treaties are cited by the Canadian and European governments as the reason why they cannot formally legalize marijuana, even as some work out policies that create de facto legalization.
See
We Are Winning! Switzerland to Surpass the Dutch and Allow Not Only Use and Sales – But Also Cultivation. Major Impact On Germany and the Rest of Europe.
and
Belgium To Decriminalize Possession and Cultivation for Personal Use. No Coffeeshops, Yet.

Now consider where the Europeans – and Canadians -- find themselves.

First, they do not like the Plan Colombia, because they see it as an attack on some of the poorest people in the world. It looks even more like " Vietnam " to them than to Americans. In any case, it is hardly a domestic DEAland matter. They are being pressured to contribute.

Second, the EU is beginning to develop its own foreign policies. An EU delegation is now visiting North Korea, trying to play " good cop, " just as Bush is taking a harder line. Most of them also are uncomfortable with Bush’s new China policy.

Third, Bush seems much less interested in global affairs than the hyperactive Clinton, who became personally involved in everything from Northern Ireland to the Middle East. In this regard, Bush is much more in keeping with historical American reticence.

Fourth, the new Bush Administration has unilaterally adopted policies, which affect them and which they do not like, especially regarding the Kyoto and ABM treaties.

Finally, many of them have decided that the Drug War -- especially marijuana prohibition -- is another manifestation of American Puritanism, on which they have always looked down.

All of these factors combine to accelerate the process of moving away from the DEAland Drug War, and especially marijuana prohibition. Recently in the Dutch Parliament the government spokesman said, " the treaties (in particular the UN treaties on this subject) can not long remain the contolling factor, but rather must be seen as subject to adaptation to the practices of the present moment. "
See
We Are Winning! The Dutch Government Shows More Confidence that Things Are Going Our Way in Europe.

Now there is more than ample precedent. Certainly no one could argue that changes in treaties regarding a country’s cannabis policies are as important to third parties as the repudiation of the Kyoto and ABM treaties.

And the problem for the prohibitionists is that when this process starts, the prohibitionist paradigm is shattered. The treaties have lost their magic, and once again Harry Anslinger has been caught lying.
